utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to our sound engineers -- Can the interpreters hear me? Yes, they can -- counsel for the Prosecution, the Defence, General Krstic. We shall today be resuming the case. For the record, we have the same situation today as yesterday; that is, the witness, who is right in the courtroom, will continue his testimony. Good morning, Witness H [sic]. You will now continue to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Judge Riad, my learned friends for the Defence. Examined by Mr. Cayley: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, just to remind you that you are under the solemn oath that you were under yesterday to speak the truth. I'll quickly refresh your memory as to where you were yesterday. You had spoken about General Mladic arriving in Potocari and essentially, in your words, mounting a propaganda exercise. We were then just about to move to General Mladic's second visit that you recalled, and I'd like you to explain to the Judges what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came up to me and wanted to speak to the UN commander at that time at that position, and that was me, of course. And he spoke to me through my interpreter, the Muslim interpreter that was originally based with Bravo Company, and we spoke about a lot of things that had nothing to do with what happened that day, about soccer and other cases. At one point, he mentioned about the multiracial composition of my unit that was there. There were a few soldiers that were Negroes that were on that position, and he stated, through my Muslim interpreter, that in ten years, the Bosnian Serb army would be in Holland to protect the Dutch from the Muslims. And I said I didn't agree with him, also through the Muslim interpreter, of course. Later on, he started to intimidate the Muslim interpreter, because he asked me who he was and why he was there. I explained to General Mladic that he was an interpreter and he had a UN pass, and at that point he started to intimidate the Muslim interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what time this was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that he started to intimidate the Muslim interpreter. Can you tell the Judges what happened to the Muslim interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic put his arm around him and he started to speak to me through the interpreter, telling that -- he played a sort of role-play, saying that the interpreter was a Serb, that he was a good guy, and that General Mladic was a Muslim, and he said, "Well, I'm a Muslim. I only think about making babies, but this guy, this interpreter is a Serb, he's a good fellow and I like him." And he put his arm around him and he practically crushed him into his own body. Later on, the UN pass that was given to the interpreter was taken away by the bodyguards of General Mladic, and I had to speak to the bodyguards to get it back. The interpreter was very scared, of course, because that was his only pass that he had that would practically ensure him of not being taken away like the other men but could stay with the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did General Mladic spend at your position in Potocari, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have been there for about an hour, I think. The conversation I had with him was maybe 15 minutes, 20 minutes, but he stayed there more in the background, speaking to Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, whilst General Mladic was there, the transportation process was continuing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular incident, while General Mladic was present, in connection with the transportation of the Muslims out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, there was a woman that was panicking, and she was really almost in a state of hysteria. So we got her out of the big group of refugees and, through the interpreter, asked what was going on with her. She said that her children, five children, were already loaded on a lorry and she had lost them in the big chaos, and she now saw them in the back of that truck, already starting to drive away from where she was. Through the interpreter that became clear to me, and I planned to get her on the truck that was already moving. The situation was that we had the refugees -- we were there in between the refugees and the Serbs, and practically no movement of UN soldiers was from our location towards the buses, because in between there were the Serb soldiers. So I asked the interpreter, I said, "Well, can you help me?" Because General Mladic was in between talking to that Serb soldier. And I said, "Go over to General Mladic, who is the highest in command, over there, explain to him what I'm doing, because I'm taking that woman up to that lorry now, and I don't know what the Serb soldiers will do, how they will react if I cross that, more or less, border." I didn't ask for his reaction. I took the woman, carried her to -- running towards the lorry, and when I put her on the lorry together with the children, and I turned around, I saw that the interpreter had gone over to General Mladic and tried to explain. So he did what I had asked him to do. So I went up to General Mladic, and at that point General Mladic was very, very mad, and he told me, also through the interpreter, that if I would ever send the interpreter up to General Mladic without it being clear that he was interpreting for me, then he would shoot him right there on the spot. At that point, the interpreter was so scared, and he was shivering all over, so I had him escorted back to the UN Compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Mladic say to you or explain to you why he would shoot the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for speaking to him as a Muslim interpreter. Just for speaking to him without it being clear that he was interpreting for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how much longer General Mladic stayed in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen him from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after General Mladic left or indeed went out of your sight, do you recall what you saw commencing in and around Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained, the situation was that we tried to calm the Muslim refugees; that, through Mane, it would be clear to me how many buses there were and how many people could go onto the bus, and then we would leave, would let them leave in little groups so that they wouldn't trample each other by rushing to the buses. So we had a little control about the buses so that there wouldn't be any overcrowding of the buses that happened in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the groups that were going towards the buses, they consisted of women and children; or men, women, and children. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, men, women, and children, but on the first day I noticed that about 50 meters behind where the UN soldiers were and where I was, men were sitting in a lawn, front lawn of a house, a small house that was near the factory sites. And I asked Mane, who was in charge there of the Serb soldiers, because it was clear to me that they were selecting the men out, why he had done that. And he said, "Well, we will bring them over to Bratunac and we will have a list of war criminals, Muslim war criminals, and we want to compare the men we have here, the names of those men, to the list we have of war criminals. And if there are war criminals, we will send them to a court; and if they are not, if they're civilians, we will send them on with the normal convoys towards Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2, which I actually believe, I think, is my copy, because the Court copy was marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the registrar is finding that exhibit, how long did those men stay on that stretch of lawn outside those houses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day, that was the first day, so that was the place where they were brought to. They stayed there the rest of the day, until the evening, when all of the convoys and deportation was stopped, and then were brought -- or taken away by a lorry. I don't know where they brought them. I could see from about a hundred meters distance that they were put into a lorry and were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you can recall, Captain van Duijn, the location where you saw these men on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a house in this neighbourhood [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could leave your pointer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness is pointing to -- I think there are two small houses under that pointer, as one looks at the photograph, to the right of the road, passing north/south in the photograph and just beneath the point of the arrow marking the Zinc Factory, perhaps two centimeters below the point of the arrow which marks the Zinc Factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain van Duijn. Can you recall from your memory at what stage the transport of Muslims ceased on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the beginning of the evening, about 6.00 in the evening, I think 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening, just before it became dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mane again that evening?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that of course the deportation stopped, the convoy stopped, the buses wouldn't come, until the next morning; that he and his soldiers would retreat to Bratunac to go and celebrate; and that he wanted us to clear the road, because a lot of refugees were still on the road, on the asphalt road, and he wanted us to clear it of refugees because they wanted to use, or other units would use that road to move troops to the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that he stated to you that he wanted the road cleared because they wanted to use -- or other units would use the road to move troops south. Which troops are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what troops they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else of significance from your memory that actually happened on that day, on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day itself or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the evening. In the evening.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, because I had been relieved by Lieutenant Koster for that night -- he would stay there in the midst of the refugees, together with other soldiers -- I myself was of course real tired, coming from the blocking position, and after that day, so I tried to get some rest, went back to the UN Compound and of course report what had happened that day to my commanders. And when I went over to the UN Compound, I saw a roll-call taking place of Serb soldiers, I presume, because I saw the little man with code-name Stalin standing in front of a unit of more or less company size, between the location I had been earlier and the UN Compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 73. You can use this copy, and then if you just give it straight back to me, then we can move more quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just indicate to the Judges, because you've mentioned him today and we mentioned him yesterday, if you could just point to the individual that you identified as Stalin.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating again on that exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 73, the individual on the right-hand side of the photograph with a moustache, wearing spectacles. Thank you, Captain van Duijn. If I could have that exhibit back. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to the next date, the 13th of July. Do you remember approximately what time you rose in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rose about 5.00 in the morning, and after seeing some soldiers that I wanted to accompany that day, I -- it was about 6.00, half past 6.00, again at the location where Lieutenant Koster was, and he told me about the things that happened during the night. And the plan was that I would take over from him at that stage again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same location that you showed the Judges yesterday on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a little bit more to the south, because I had spoken to Lieutenant Koster on the evening of the first day of the deportations, and it was very difficult for us to try and keep the refugees calm. So I spoke to him and I said, "Well, I think we should make a sort of tunnel for the refugees to come in with APCs, formed with APCs," so the distance we had to cover with UN soldiers would be smaller, so we could easily -- more easily could contain them and keep them calm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Koster speak to you about what had happened during the night?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that a few incidents had happened, but the most memorable incidents were that a man had hung himself in the factory and they had to get the body down from the place where he had hung himself; and that another man had injured himself in total panic, hitting himself with a rock on his head, trying to become injured so he could be taken up to the hospital so he would be transported with the sick people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you recall from when you took over from Koster, what happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serb soldiers and Mane were not there at that time, he had said to me that he would be there about 8.00 or somewhere in the vicinity of that time. But the bus drivers and the buses were already there, so I decided to keep the families together and to send everyone on the bus with the groups they wanted. We already started, because the buses and the bus drivers knew where they had to drive, because they had been there the day before as well. We already started the transports for about an hour or something. And then the Serbs came and Mane took over again. And from that moment on, the men were singled out again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did the Bosnian Serb army return to Potocari? Do you recall approximately?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must be between 8.00 and 8.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the transportation process go on all day long?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended about 4.00, because by then all of the people of the big group of refugees had left by then, about 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the scene to the Judges after all of the refugees had been transported out of Potocari, what you saw in and around the UN compound and indeed the factory and bus sites.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The factory sites were covered with goods that people had tried to take with them: bags of potatoes, blankets, all of the things they had tried to take with them as they fled. All the factory sites were covered in personal belongings as well, even pictures and stuff like that that they had left behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims left at all?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men, on the second day, when they were singled out, were taken up to a house we called the White House, almost opposite of the entrance of the UN Compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt, Captain van Duijn?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a photograph that I showed, I think, the day before yesterday. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the White House, only in the time we were there, there were much more trees and bushes that more or less covered the front lawn of that White House.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you saw at the White House?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The White House itself was packed with men of different ages, and there were a few refugees in front of the house but most of them were packed inside. I only stayed standing in front of the White House and having a peek inside, but I didn't go to the back. So I don't know what was there on the back side of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the appearance of those men that you saw at the White House?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were packed together, and because it was very warm, they were sweating. They were very, very scared. Some of them were shivering. Some of the men were speaking themselves, but you could easily see that they were very, very scared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything else at the White House apart from these men that were packed inside and outside the White House?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came up to the White House, and as you can see, in the front of the White House there is a large lawn, it was covered totally with personal belongings, with pictures, holiday snapshots, as well as passports and other identity papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you'd seen this, did you speak to anybody about what you'd seen at the White House?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mane again, because the first day of the deportations when I noticed that the men were singled out I asked him why, and he gave me the explanation of them wanting to distinguish who was a war criminal and who was not. So I asked him again, because I saw all the passports and identity papers, why they couldn't take them with them, because that was in front of the house and not on the men itself. He said, "Well, they don't need the stuff that's there. They don't need it any more." Then I asked him how he could explain the fact that if they wanted to know who was a war criminal and who was not they could do that without identity papers, because if they would give a false name, it wouldn't be on the list of war criminals, and the person would go free and join the rest of the convoy to Tuzla. Then he more or less laughed at me and said, "Well, don't make such a fuss out of it. They just don't need their passports any more."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think at that point, Captain van Duijn?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realised that the story he had told me before was not true any more, or hadn't been true at all, and at that moment, I realised that something bad was going to happen to the men, and the only thing I can recollect now is I thought about the things I had seen before on television, before I went to Bosnia, about concentration camps and men being sent to camps like that. At least I knew that they were not going to be sent with a convoy when they were not on the list. They would just be sent on a convoy to Tuzla, and that wasn't true at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the transportation process that you saw taking place, is there any image or memory that remains with you above any other after these years have passed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an incident of a family that consisted of about six to eight women, from an old woman about in her 60s, 70s until a young girl about 12 years old, I think, and you could see that there were different generations. With that family there was only one man, and he was about 45 to 50 years old, but he looked fit and in shape. During the periods of the deportations, every time a man was singled out because of Mane telling me about they wanted to get to the warriors and the war criminals, whenever a man was singled out or a boy was singled out that was practically too old or too young to be a soldier, I spoke to Mane and protested with him. I said, "Well, you can't be serious. That can't be a soldier. That can't be a war criminal," and every time I protested, he would let them go with their families. During the incident, I told you about the family that consisted of almost practically all women, and the one man, I didn't protest because he was the classical borderline case, where you could easily tell that he could be a soldier or he was just on the borderline, and I made the decision at that point not to protest and he was singled out. I know, of course, that if I would have protested with every man that was singled out, no one could stay with his family, and every man was singled out. Every boy was singled out. But I had to make a decision at that time, and I made the decision not to protest, and the man was singled out, and I think that will stay with me the rest of my life, that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now, very briefly, go back to April of 1995, and I think at that point you were a commander on two observation posts, were you not?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Judges which observation posts those were?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the northeast, Sector 4 of the enclave. They were Observation Posts Quebec and Romeo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there were Serb forces opposite your observation posts, and could you very briefly tell the Judges what you observed in April 1995 that happened with those Serb forces, what changes you saw taking place.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had good contact with OP Romeo with the soldiers that were stationed near there, about 200 metres from the location of OP Romeo. We called that the Dragan bunker, named after the first Serb commander that was stationed there. And we could see from March, April on, that the Serb forces that were there in the beginning consisted of old men, shabby clothes, with only handguns, and they were quite nice to my soldiers that were on OP Romeo. And from March, April on, there were reinforcements taking place. Every Tuesday there would come a bus. First, January, February, it was to relieve and replace the men that were inside the bunker, but from March, April on, there would come reinforcements, and the men that were there stayed there and they were only brought in new troops. And the troops that were brought in were much better uniformed, polished their shoes, maintained their weapons, did some maintenance, and you could see that there was more or less a sort of build-up, and we reported it to our commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, if you could talk about Muslim forces within the enclave. If you could tell the Judges what you observed from your position at those two observation posts of Muslim forces within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a lot of contact with the second in command. He told me that he was from the Northern Brigade of the Muslims. His name was Nasir Sabanovic, and he was the local commander for my two observation posts from the Muslim forces. They did a lot of work to make trenches and bunkers near the observation posts or just behind my observation post. Nasir Sabanovic -- at that time I was on OP Quebec myself -- came up to the OP to tell me what he was thinking about the situation and also told me about his patrols that he went on, accompanied by two or three other Muslim soldiers, when he was going out of the enclave into Serb territory to do reconnaissance patrols or, as he stated to me, that he placed mines on the roads towards the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your location, how many Muslim soldiers did you see at your two observation posts?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the two OPs that I was at, there must have been about 50 to 100 Muslim soldiers in that vicinity in the later period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were armed with handguns, with Kalashnikovs, and 1 out of 10 or 1 out of 15 had a rocket launcher of some sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also report to you any risk that there was to your two observation posts from Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He warned me about that because of the location of my OPs were the closest to Serb positions in the enclave, he said that there was a plan of the Serbs to take over the two OPs, two of my OPs, and he said that through his patrols he had stationed mines and placed mines. So the initial threat was now gone, but he was still afraid of the Serbs taking over my OPs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which indeed happened eventually.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, yes. Eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's just go back to what you saw taking place in July of 1995, and this is the final questions that I have for you. You are a Captain in the Dutch army. Do you regularly go on military training exercises?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on a lot of exercises throughout my career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what levels have you gone on exercise? At what level of military formation have you been on exercise?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Platoon, company, battalion, and even big brigade or divisional exercises in Denmark or Germany or Greece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you look back at what you saw taking place in the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995, can you estimate, from your experience, at what level that operation was taking place, now that you look back?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I've read about what had taken place and read about the number of Serb soldiers that were involved in their whole operation, but when you look at the piece of terrain, a very difficult part of terrain with only one road that's covered with asphalt, my opinion is that it should be at least on a divisional level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your recollection --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By NATO standards, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, by NATO standards. And by that you mean the way NATO addresses particular military formations, how it labels those formations?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your recollection, do you remember what the higher military formation was in the Bosnian Serb army that was responsible for the area of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember from the beginning on that there was a unit called the Drina Wolves or the Drina Corps north of the enclave, and according to the conversations I had with Mane, who also told me that he was, with his military police unit, sort of a liaison or a part of the Drina Wolves, I suspected that that was the Drina Wolves that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say the Drina Wolves, which was a unit, but I'm actually interested in the larger formation, and you mentioned the Drina Corps. Which was the larger military formation that was in the area?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's now, as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the nickname used for the Drina Corps was the Drina Wolves, as far as I know. So when I mention the Drina Wolves, I mean the Drina Corps and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much indeed, Captain van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. I can offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Petrusic, Witness H [sic], you're now going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Petrusic, who is representing General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning colleagues from the Prosecution. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Captain. After the 13th of July, how long did you and your unit stay in the base, that is, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed for a couple of more days, and I believe we returned to Zagreb on the 20th of July. I don't know the exact date any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm very sorry to interrupt you, but I can see in the transcript that we -- that somebody referred to Witness H, but the witness in question is Captain van Duijn and not Witness H. I can see this in line 6 on page 22, and this will have to be corrected. Sorry, Mr. Petrusic. You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, Captain, did you ever go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague Mr. Cayley, you said that there was a unit that operated in the area of Srebrenica, a unit which belonged to the VRS. Can you be more specific and explain to us whether between the unit that you referred to as Drina Wolves and the Drina Corps, as a larger military unit, whether there was any smaller unit between the two which would still belong to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only smaller unit I know of was the military police unit where Captain Mane was in. That was more or less attached to the Drina Wolves or Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Captain van Duijn. Your Honours, I do not have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Cayley, do you have any further additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, good morning?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll just ask you from the end, because the learned Defence counsel asked if you had been to Srebrenica. You mentioned yesterday, at the beginning of your testimony, that you saw scenes in Srebrenica, smoke coming from houses, shelling, and the panic of the people. You saw it in Srebrenica itself or you saw it from a distance?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I -- at that period, I was in the blocking position south of Srebrenica, and I saw it taking place in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The city itself.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the south I could look down on the city of Srebrenica, and I could see smoke coming from the houses and houses being hit by shelling. To my knowledge, the question that was asked by the Defence was about the period after the fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. So you were close enough to see all this.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We have your description. It's there, so I don't need to ask about it any more. You referred to the conversation with Mane when he was telling you that they needed these men for inquiry to find out if they committed war crimes, and you told them, "Then why don't they keep their papers because the papers will be essential." He told you they do not need their identity papers any more.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Laughingly. So what was your conclusion? What was the meaning of that for you as a responsible UN officer?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that at least the story that he had told me about trying to single out the war criminals was not true, so they would more or less treat all the men in the same way, the same terrible way. At that point, I radioed to the OPs room and said, "Well, we have to transport. We have to send vehicles with transportation of the men. We have to be there, whatever happens." I tried, myself, tried to get into the bus but was pulled away by Mane and also at gunpoint from a soldier that blocked the entrance of the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: At the end of your testimony, you referred to the Drina Corps and the Drina Wolves, which you consider it almost identical, but you didn't mention much about them. What do you know about this Drina Corps during this period when you were in charge?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the intel we had before we went to Bosnia, where they said "Well, the Drina Corps was stationed there." We must have been -- must have had lessons about their insignias or ranks, but I don't recollect that any more. The only thing I was thinking about again was during the conversation with Mane, when he told me that he was part of the Drina Corps with his military unit. So that's the things I know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He was part of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was more or less part of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Mr. Stalin, was he part of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of Mane, so I presume he was also in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any actions which justified calling him Mr. Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You know what Stalin did?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what Stalin did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it related to the kind of actions which Stalin did?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Mane what his real name was instead of Stalin, but Mane didn't answer about it, he just said his radio name or his radio nickname is Stalin and that's the only thing I know about that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was he high in grade, Mr. Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was higher than Mane and Mane told me he was a Captain. So I presume that he was major or something, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But he had higher authorities than him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had higher authorities than Mane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean Stalin was not the chief of everything?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was not the man giving orders?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you know who was giving orders around the whole place apart from Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my location, it was Mane, and because Stalin, the man we'd nicknamed Stalin was the commander of Mane, I presumed that Stalin was giving orders to Mane about a larger area, but I don't know who was giving orders in the whole of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The part of the White House and where you had this --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was Stalin and Mane?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you met Mladic. Did you ever meet General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I recollect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nor see him around, see him moving around, giving orders?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you were talking to Mladic, this very significant conversation, which was very unclear to me, you said at a certain moment he hugged the interpreter and told you he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then he would say he would kill him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He played a sort of a role-play at first with the Muslim interpreter, embarrassing him by saying, well -- and he hugged him like this with his arm around him, crushing him to his own body, and he said, "Do you know him?" And I said, "Well, of course I know him, because he's my interpreter. He said, "No, he's not your interpreter. He's not a Muslim. He's a Serb. He's a good guy." And Mladic, General Mladic, then pointed to himself and he said, "Well, I am a Muslim, and I only think about making babies, so I am a bastard. But this guy is a good guy." So he pretended that the Muslim was a Serb and he himself was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was some kind of changing roles.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sort of a role-playing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And making fun, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to embarrass the Muslim interpreter, who was of course very scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then he added that he would be coming -- he would be defending Holland against the Muslim invasion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He saw a few of my soldiers sitting, and he actually shook hands with him, and there were two white soldiers and one Negro soldier. And then he said, "Well, is he from Holland too?" And I explained to him that we have a very multiracial society in Holland. And then General Mladic said, "Well, that's not good, and in ten years the Bosnian Muslim army will be in Holland to protect you from the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was not good that Holland has a multiracial society or something. I think that he meant that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He wanted ethnic cleansing in Holland, or what?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Captain, I should also like to ask a few questions of you. You spoke about the period of April 1995 and about the changes that you could observe from your observation posts Q and R. You also spoke about propaganda which was conducted by General Mladic. My question in respect to that is as follows: Before these events, had there been any propaganda by Serbs in the enclave of Srebrenica, if you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my recollection. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you to clarify something with my next question. Speaking of the Drina Corps and Drina Wolves, is it one and the same thing or are we speaking about two different things here? Because I thought that you said that Drina Wolves was just a nickname for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that Drina Wolves is a nickname for Drina Corps, and so they -- the two mean the same thing, in my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You also spoke about the White House. You said that there had been a pile of documents, passports, personal belongings of people who were in the White House. Do you know, by any chance, what has happened with all those things?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The days after all of the events had taken place and we were back in the UN Compound, we could see a lot of people coming from Bratunac and more or less looting everything that was usable from all of the houses, and we could also see that at the location of the White House, stuff was brought together and burnt, and that's when I remembered that possibly all of the papers and all of the passports were burnt at that time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who burnt those documents and passports?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Captain. You have provided a lot of information, lots of clarification for us. Let me just verify if there are any documents that we have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecution Exhibit 71, 72, 73, and 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the situation with them? Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, those are a series of four photographs that the witness recognised and indeed provided foundation for their admission, so I would apply to you for admission of those photographs into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, or Mr. Visnjic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not. At the same time, I should like to take this opportunity -- I don't know whether you're now going to have a break or if we're going to continue with the proceedings, but after we have liberated the witness, and before the next witness comes into the courtroom, the Defence should like to have 10 or 15 minutes for two oral motions. So if we could kindly have that opportunity, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. The documents have been admitted into evidence. Captain van Duijn, thank you very much once again on behalf of the International Criminal Tribunal for coming here to testify. We understand that you have been through quite an ordeal while you were still very young, and I hope that you will continue to enjoy this multiracial, multiethnical atmosphere in this beautiful country of yours. Thank you very much. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me just tell you that we have something at around 11.00. We are not able to continue before 11.10. So I think that it's much better to deal with the motions of the Defence now, and then after that we will have a break, and after the break we will continue with the witness. We have this commitment around 11.00. If we didn't have it, we could continue right away, but I think that it's better in this situation to organise our break around 11.00. So let us hear Mr. Visnjic. Let us hear your motion. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Our motions are in a way interrelated, but we nevertheless separated them, and I shall now submit the first one. The Defence would like the Chamber to rule on a problem which arose with regard to the statements of the witnesses for the Prosecution, and to pass a ruling to resolve the matter in a principled manner. Before I do that, I should like to remind the Chamber that both the Defence and the Prosecution for the last two months before the beginning of the trial had done a great deal of work regarding the disclosure of evidence, so that on the eve of the trial, the Defence found itself with a very large quantity of evidence on its hands disclosed by the Prosecution, and that includes also witness statements, both in English and in Serbo-Croatian. Some of these statements we also received after the trial began. For reasons that Your Honours already know, the summaries of the witness statements we received a week before the trial began. On the other hand, the change of schedule of the hearings, and of course we do understand that it is a forced measure, has precluded the Defence to go through this evidence and to verify all the evidence that it received during the period that I have just mentioned. Needless to say, we're all trying to somehow reconcile the principle of expediency with the principle of the right to defence. And of late, some witnesses, in their testimony before the Chamber, have begun describing incidents which were not mentioned in their earlier statements, and that is a completely new situation now so far as the Defence counsel are concerned, and we were unable to go through these statements without a special investigation. In light of all this, with regard to those witnesses and the witnesses whose statements we received within some 60 days before the beginning of the trial, we should like to request the Chamber to pass a ruling, to pass a decision, to allow the Defence, as a matter of principle, to, subject to supplementary investigation to be conducted by the Defence, to therefore permit the Defence to call back a certain witness -- of course, depending on whatever it is established by the additional investigation -- to call back the witness and have him give evidence regarding the newly arisen facts. So this is a principled motion, and we would, needless to say, make such submissions in every individual case, following, of course, following the decision of the Chamber, if the Chamber makes such a ruling as we are now asking you to do. We are governed in this by Rule 65 ter (E) (iv), Roman (iv), and 66(A)(ii) and Article 21, 4(A) and (B), of the Statute of the Tribunal. That would be our first motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you said, Mr. Visnjic, these applications are interrelated, but you wanted to do it separately. Perhaps we could indeed treat them severally; that is, you can hear the Prosecutor's statements and then submit your application. That is, also perhaps we could hear the answer of the Prosecution, or rather the reaction of the Prosecution. What do you think, Mr. Harmon, about this application? However, before that -- excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Before that, have you discussed the matter with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, not in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But we have already established that Rule before any motion is presented, but we should hear the opinion of the other party and whether they agree or do not agree. If they agree, very well; if not, we can try to reach an agreement, an understanding. But we now have to hear the view of the Prosecutor, and we also have a break. And during the break, of course, it is also possible to shed views on various matters. But since the Chamber is not sitting in full, we shall not be able to make a ruling now; that is, the Chamber has not yet passed another decision which is also pending. We shall therefore await for Judge Wald to return in order to pass the decision, and we shall also need the presence of Judge Wald to decide on this matter as well. But we shall hear all this matter, and the Chamber will then discuss. Today we cannot pass that decision, because Judge Wald is not with us. But be that as it may, I should like to hear the opinion of Mr. Harmon in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Judge Riad; good morning, counsel. My first observation is somewhat similar to yours. If the second motion is related to the first motion, I think perhaps they should be explored together. There may be an interrelationship that might affect the answer that I give. So if I could invite counsel to give the second part of his motion, I'm happy to respond to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We appreciate your suggestion, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, I have to go back to what I just said. It was perhaps preferable to hear both applications so that we could address them both at the same time. Could we hear your second application, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we submitted a motion regarding the text of the indictment, and we had certain objections against some of the Prosecution evidence. You made a ruling in that respect, and I am not commenting on that. However, after that, the Registry gave us a certificate explaining to us that the Serbian text of the indictment, the one that was available to Mr. Petrusic and me, was erroneously translated. It had to do with our previous motion. Article 18.4 of the Statute of the Tribunal in this regard says that when the Prosecutor determines that there is a prima facie case, he, that is, the Prosecutor, shall prepare an indictment containing a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged under the Statute. This means that every count in the indictment with which the accused is charged should relate to specific definitions in the Statute. At the same time, Article 21 stipulates that the accused shall be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands. At the same time, Rule 47(G) says that if the accused does not understand either of the official languages of the Tribunal, a translation of the indictment in that language shall also be prepared in the language that the accused understands and which will make part or be included as part of each certified copy of the indictment. These provisions were adopted so that the accused would be informed about the accusations, about the charges made against him, and the case which he needs to prepare in this defence, in the language which he, that is, the accused, understands. These provisions also impose certain limitations, certain limits on the evidence to be used in the proceedings before the Chamber. Specifically, we are in a situation now where the Prosecutors have done properly their part of the job. The English and the French versions of the indictment were handled in an appropriate manner, that is, in a manner corresponding to the manner in which the Prosecution prepared their evidence. On the other hand, it is evident that for, if I may call them technical reasons, the Defence has been, and especially the defendant, has been in a way denied one of its fundamental rights. Mr. President, we looked at this situation carefully and we believe that the accused has suffered certain damage, that his rights have been prejudiced in a certain way, and we thought about how this situation could be remedied. The Defence believes that it could be set right if additional time were allotted for the investigation at the three sites which are called into question due to this misunderstanding, I'll call it. I do not wish to go now into the timetable, into the time schedule of the Chamber, but the application for the supplementary time I shall submit when the Prosecution closes its case, since we already announced such a possibility. So basically, our second application is as follows: We first wish to clarify the situation that we are in now; and secondly, the Defence, subsequent to its application for this additional investigation, the Defence will apply to be allotted that additional time, because if one reads the Serbo-Croatian text which we had, it is quite clear that only the sites listed in the indictment are the subject of the charges. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe the time has now come for our break. Before we make the break, I should like to hear who will be our next witness. Are any protective measures sought, what kind of protective measures? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our next witness will be Colonel Kingori, and no protective measures will be sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will also use the break. As I told you, we have an obligation around 11.00, so if we could make a half-hour break, and the parties can meet now that the Prosecutor knows the substance of the application or applications of the Defence, you could perhaps meet and discuss it before the next witness is called. You can also talk to the Chamber and let us know what are your views, whether you agree with that or not. If you do not agree, then the Chamber will take the decision on the motion, on the application of the Defence. Now we shall have a break of half an hour, that is, until 11.20, until twenty past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming here, Witness. Let us first hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, we have somewhat changed the order of the day. I will explain this later on. Witness, thank you very much for coming to testify here. You will begin by answering questions put to you by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could first ask the usher to move the ELMO back so I can see the witness, I would appreciate it. Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, can you state your full name and spell your last name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: My name is Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph Gichuhi Kingori. I spell the last name K-i-n-g-o-r-i.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you're a career military officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your nationality is Kenyan?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been in the Kenyan Air Force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I joined the Kenyan Air Force in 1977. That means by now I've been there for over 23 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, Colonel Kingori, did you serve as a United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in that capacity in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges what is the role of a United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Physically, Your Honour, as a military observer -- we used to call them U-N-M-O, that is UNMOs -- you are there to monitor the violations to the ceasefire agreement, and also you are supposed to be neutral and bring the warring factions together. This could have been by means of holding meetings with either side and bringing whatever you're told from one side to the other, so as to bring them as close as possible to each other. Also if there was anything to be conveyed from the UN headquarters, it used to pass through us. Likewise, we also had to convey whatever we get from the warring factions to the UN headquarters through the UNMO channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your principal role as an UNMO to observe materials that related to the military and related to ceasefire violations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you had to report up the normal chain, can you tell the Judges what was the chain of your reporting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the normal chain was from the UNMO sector, that is, from where we were. We write the report to the UNMO headquarters. Like in Srebrenica our headquarters was in Tuzla. So we relayed the message to Tuzla, and then they would relay the same to the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb. Then that is formally transmitted to the UN headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, can you explain to the Judges the difference between an UNMO and a soldier who was serving in the former Yugoslavia as a part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said concerning UNMO, the main roles was to monitor any violations to the ceasefire agreement and also handle military matters. Also you are to do some humanitarian issues, like helping the aged, helping those who are injured, analysing craters, that is, a crater analysis, in case of any impacts using heavy weapons, and then send the same to the headquarters to the channel that I gave you. As for UNPROFOR, UNPROFOR, one thing to note is that they were armed. They had arms and they were staying in their battalion headquarters of various outposts, as required in their observation posts and all that. The difference comes whereby we are not supposed to use arms, because we did not have any. But for the UNPROFOR, in case of anything, they could have used arms. Hence the difference in that we, as almost who are neutral -- we are supposed to be as neutral as possible -- hence the requirement that we stay together with the people in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not -- when you were serving as an UNMO officer, you were not at the same location and quartered with UNPROFOR soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were staying separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did UNPROFOR have a different mandate than you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they had a different mandate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to describe their mandate as opposed to your mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, their mandate was, as a requirement of the UNPROFOR headquarters, to also monitor, but relate the military activities to what they had been told to do. That is, in case of any activity from the warring factions, they could be called in to act against the source of the fire. With us, we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did UNPROFOR have a principal role in ensuring the provision of humanitarian aid to various locations in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Repeat your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the principal roles, as opposed to your role, which dealt almost exclusively with military matters, was UNPROFOR's role different in that it was to ensure, or attempt to ensure, that humanitarian aid would flow to various parts in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as an UNMO, how long did you serve in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stayed there for one year: six months in East Krajina, that is, Sector 8; and then four months in Srebrenica; and the remaining period was in Sector south, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive your assignment to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was towards the end of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you actually arrive in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I arrived in Srebrenica somewhere around -- I think it was 4th or 5th. I'm not very sure of the actual dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 4th or 5th of which month?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Of April 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived, where were you headquartered?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, our headquarters was in the PTT building in Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived, how many other UNMOs were also in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were five other UNMOs, and with me that made six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they there, the other UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can remember one was from Canada, there was one from Ukraine, there was one from Ghana, one from Holland, and the other one was from -- where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the other from Brazil?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: From Brazil, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time the enclave fell in July of 1995, how many UNMOs were in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, it's good to inform you that for the UNMOs, we were to stay in one place for one month, and then we go out for leave or vacation for six days, then go back to continue with the work. At this time there were three UNMOs who were supposed to be rotated, and one of them had stayed there for I think four months or so. When his time came, he was not allowed to leave the enclave. The second one, who was supposed to leave the following month, was not given clearance by the Serbs to leave the enclave, and so the same happened to that one. That means just before the war started, the three were allowed to leave the enclave, but unfortunately there was no replacement allowed to go into the enclave by the Serbs. That means we were left, only three of us: that is me, from Kenya; David Tetteh from Ghana; and Andryk, from Holland. But it's worth noting that by this time Andryk was admitted in the DutchBat hospital, so we were only two in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as part of your duties, you had to get to know contacts from the various warring factions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention on the Bosnian Serb army. Could you tell the Judges who were your points of contact from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the Bosnian Serbs -- that is, we used to call them the BSA -- we were contacting directly with Major Nikolic and at times with a colonel called Vukovic, through our interpreter, who was called Petar. And something to remember is that when we were to meet with any other person, Major Nikolic was always there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did Major Nikolic dress?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Major Nikolic was always dressed in combat dress; that is, camouflage, green; green camouflage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was Colonel Vukovic dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Vukovic was dressed the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what position you believed Major Nikolic to have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Major Nikolic was, as we were told, in charge of one of the units, one of the fighting units on the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what his higher military formation was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way the BSA was organised was that there were superior officers above him, and all that chain went, as far as I know, up to General Mladic level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me about Colonel Vukovic. How did he represent himself to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Vukovic was also in charge of one of the brigades, which I do not remember which one, and he was actually -- the way he was -- he was actually senior to Major Nikolic, the way he presented himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your view, both Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic were from brigades that were around the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to describe to the Judges the attitude that you observed in Colonel Vukovic in respect of the Muslims who resided in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Vukovic -- okay. I don't know the right word, but he was a bit rough as far as the Muslims were concerned, because even at one of the meetings that we had, it was said that the Muslims have to leave Srebrenica enclave in total. He doesn't want to see them there. And if they are there, he might end up killing one of them. He once said that. So I can say he was a bit rough as far as the Muslims are concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to the Muslim side. Can you tell the Judges the representatives the Muslim military formations that you had contact with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were contacting with the chief of staff, who was, I remember, Ramiz Becirovic. Then there was the intelligence officer, IO for short, who was called Ekrem Salihovic or someone like that. Then there was the mayor, the deputy mayor, and the president of the opstina. Those are the main people that we were contacting with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your contacts with these Muslim representatives, what was their attitude in respect of the Serbs who were outside of the enclave? How did they express themselves to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Muslims, in whichever meeting that we had, were always afraid of what the Serbs around them would do or could do to them. They were in constant fear that they might overrun the enclave and maybe even harass them. But as far as military activities, there was very little military activities, only when they used to go to look for food outside. They were always afraid that something could happen to them on the way, because there was not enough food in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a rough attitude of Colonel Vukovic. Did you see a similar rough attitude in the representatives of the Muslim community with whom you were dealing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori, let me ask you in terms of how you would conduct your business. If there was an allegation of a ceasefire violation, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing I would do is to request for more information, especially concerning the actual location where the violation has occurred. Then go to that particular place, see what violation has occurred. By "seeing," I mean maybe if it was some rocket or artillery shell had fallen at that place, I would go and see the actual location, maybe analyse the crater to know the source of the artillery piece. Then using the maps that we had, know the source, where it actually came from that is, and get it in terms of grid references so that we can forward it to the UN headquarters through the normal channels. But if it was a violation of maybe some normal shooting, which was prevalent in that area, mainly from the BSA side, I would also interview the locals. I would interview them, ask them what actually transpired, who actually infiltrated into that particular area, who they believe those guys were after, and after getting all that, I would forward it to the UNMO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Colonel Kingori, that from the time you arrived in the enclave until the fall of the enclave, you spent a considerable period of your time in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is very true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were in the field, were you observing and making assessments of the various capabilities of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's very true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if there was a violation of a ceasefire or there was an incident or there was a shelling, you mentioned you prepared reports. Those were reports that were prepared by you personally or prepared by part of your team or both?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, these reports were being prepared by either me or the other UNMOs, or at times we could draft them together. What used to happen was that when you are in the field, you come with what you have found. Maybe someone else was in a different area, and maybe the other guys who are left, the other UNMOs who are left in there -- in the office. So we would combine all these and make one report and send it to the UNMO headquarters. So it was a combination of all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We'll return to the issue of reports in a few minutes. Now, let me ask you: When the Bosnian Serb side wanted to contact you, how would they do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the BSA side, they would contact our interpreter, that is, Petar, and since he had a radio, one of the radios with a frequency, he would contact us using that radio and tell us that one of them wanted to meet us, the location, that is, where he would like to meet us, and then we would confirm our availability, and just go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 42 placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, there's an image of an individual that's been placed on the ELMO. Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was our interpreter, Mr. Petar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was your --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The Serb interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your initial source of contact. When the Serbs wanted a meeting at UNMOs, they would go through Petar?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you: In the meetings that you had with the representatives of the Bosnian Serb army, from the time you arrived in the enclave in April until the time that the enclave fell, did the Bosnian Serbs complain to you about attacks being made by armed units, Muslim units from within the enclave going out of the enclave and attacking either military formations or civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not remember of any single time that the BSA complained about firing from that side, except maybe once, but that was not firing, it was the people now going to Zepa to look for food. There was nothing like military activities from the BiH side that was complained about the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the Serbs ever explain to you, in the time that you were in Srebrenica, about Serbian casualties, either civilian or military, that were the result of attacks by Muslim soldiers who had been within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me go to the other side of the conflict. Can you tell the Judges: Did the Muslim representatives complain to you about attacks by Serbs coming into the enclave, either personally by infantry formation or by artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this happened several times, very many times. The reports we could receive either from the military organisation or from locals coming from the other sides, other villages of Srebrenica, and most of the time we would even go there and find people maybe have been hit by shells. We would later take them to hospital, and analyse the craters, or just leave them there if their injuries are not serious. But the violations were more from the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims then complain to you about civilian casualties that had been suffered and did you, in fact, confirm the existence of civilian casualties on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was almost the order of the day. Most of the time we would get complaints of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you were a neutral party, but can you give the Judges your assessment of which of the warring factions appeared to you to be the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
