utterances.text: Your Honour, from what I have said and what I observed when I was there, most of the violations were against the Muslims. I can't remember of any that was against the Serbs from the Muslims. So that means, basically, the BSA are the ones who were most of time there actually the aggressors, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given the fact that you have testified that you spent a considerable period of your time in the field within the enclave, could you kindly give the Judges your assessment of the Bosnian military formations that were within the enclave? First of all, can you describe the types of equipment that you saw them in possession of?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you confirm whether you mean the Bosnian Serbs or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I made a mistake. I meant the Bosnian Muslims who were within the enclave. Can you provide the Judges with an assessment of those military formations, and when you give that assessment, can you include all aspects of military analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the Muslim side, that is BiH, there was no organised military as such. For one, it is good to remember that they did not have heavy weapons. All the heavy weapons had been withdrawn and taken to DutchBat for safe custody, because the whole enclave was a safe area. It was a demilitarised zone. That means all the weapons, especially the heavy weapons, were withdrawn and taken to DutchBat for safe custody. In fact, most of it was in the B-Company Compound near where we were living. Okay. We cannot discount the fact that they had some small arms. We're talking about AK-47s and all that, but they did not have heavy weapons. They were not -- as we can say militarily, they were not armed as such. They were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any formations of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember seeing any formation. Okay. At times you could see one, two soldiers with some small arms, but the biggest number I ever saw was a maximum of ten, and those are very few soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you assess their command structure?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can say is that their command structure -- okay. We can say it existed, but it sort of -- it was not fully established. They had a chief of staff who was Ramiz. They had someone -- I can't remember what his name was. He was a senior person whom I never met. But you cannot call that an organised military command structure. It was not exactly that. Okay, they had an IO, an intelligence officer, that is Ekrem, but it was not an organised structure the way the military should be, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assessment, Colonel Kingori, of the threat that these armed Muslims within the enclave posed to the areas outside of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think they posed any threat at all. They were not armed as such, and as compared to what I knew the BSA had or what they showed later that they had, definitely the Muslims were no match for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't we address your attention then to what the Bosnian Serb army had. Can you describe that army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least the Serbs -- I can say they had an organised structure, and they used to follow it. At the same time, I can also say they were armed with heavy weapons. At least they had artillery, because they used it. They had mortars. They had machine-guns. They had rockets, even indicated at some times where their rocket launchers were. They had tanks and many other types of heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have armoured personnel carriers? Did they have jeeps?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they had them. Later on, anyway. They robbed some from the UNPROFOR, but that was just in addition to what they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you assess or provide the Judges with an assessment on the command structure? Was it a command structure that, in your opinion, functioned and functioned properly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, their command structure functioned. The way it was organised was a normal, we can say conventional military, and you could see -- sometimes they could tell you, "I cannot be able to answer you this until I check with our higher commanders." That means they had an organised command structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did it appear to you that the Bosnian Serb army was an entity that was that one where the higher levels would issue orders and the lower subordinate units would follow orders?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the case. The higher commanders used to give orders and the lower ones used to obey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, I'd like to focus your attention on a meeting that occurred in June of 1995 and took place at the Hotel Fontana with representatives of the Bosnian Serb army. Do you recall that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that that meeting was called?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that meeting was called through by Major Nikolic, through our interpreter, Petar, and we went to the Hotel Fontana for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you personally attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the Bosnian Serb side, who was present?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the BSA side there was Major Nikolic, Colonel Vukovic, and some other senior officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4 and ask you if this particular man in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4 was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can use my exhibit right here, it might be faster. If that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see anybody in that exhibit, Colonel Kingori, who was also present; and if so, can you point him out?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular individual was in the meeting [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, on Prosecutor's 28/4, Colonel Kingori has identified the individual who is in the foreground with an orange face. He is the second individual from the right-hand side of the photograph. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have my exhibit back, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Could the witness perhaps try to remember that person's name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at present that person's name?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember the name, but -- I cannot remember the actual name, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what the purpose of that meeting was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of that meeting was mainly to discuss the people in the enclave and -- yes, I think it was mainly to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what was said at that particular meeting in respect of the people in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was said that the people in the enclave should leave the enclave as -- you know, what they said was that they do not belong there; they should leave the enclave in totality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall who was saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was said by Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any statements that you interpreted to be menacing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the words he used that time were menacing, if I can say, because he said if the Muslims do not leave, he is going to kill all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did any of the Bosnian Serb military people who were present -- or strike that. Were other Bosnian Serb military personnel present when Colonel Vukovic said that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other senior officers were also present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the other senior Bosnian Serb military officers who were present when Colonel Vukovic said that disagree with him or attempt to soften that in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, no one objected to what Colonel Vukovic said, no one talked about it, and it is as if what he said is something they had discussed earlier, or he was just conveying what they had discussed earlier or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a discussion that included a discussion about safe passage of the Muslims from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true. He said that -- it was said that if the Muslims decide to leave, as they were requested to do, they would be given a safe passage to leave through up to Tuzla, to join their brothers in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the conclusion of this meeting, Colonel Kingori, did you form any opinions about the intentions of the Bosnian Serb army? Did you walk away from that meeting with any particular feelings?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the feelings that I got out of that meeting was that maybe something was afoot, something was being planned, something to make sure that whatever Colonel Vukovic said will be done; that is, the Serbs -- the Muslims should leave the enclave and they will be given a free passage, and if they do not, maybe something will be done. We suspected something could be done, and they conveyed the same to the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me fast-forward a bit to the attack on the enclave itself. When the attack on the enclave started, where were you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was in the PTT building. We were asleep at that time, me and Major Tetteh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in the PTT building from the time the attack started until approximately the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we stayed -- okay. We did not stay inside the building, because we were going out to check what is happening. We were also going out to analyse the craters, that is, carrying out our normal onward duties. Then we would go back to the PTT building, write the sitreps, that is, the situation reports, and send them over as they occurred. And during that period, if there is anything else, we would still go out and come back with the same thing. But basically I can say we were in Srebrenica and we stayed there until much later, when we left for DutchBat Compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, first of all, Mr. President, that Prosecutor's Exhibit 77 be distributed. And Your Honours, Prosecutor's 77 are a series of UNMO reports and UNPROFOR reports between the dates of the 6th of July and the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori, have you seen these reports before? Have I shown you these reports, and did you recognise these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were these reports that were prepared by you or other members of -- Major Tetteh, who was the other UNMO, at or about the time the events described in the reports were occurring?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do these reports contain your observations as you best knew them at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, excuse me for interrupting you, but would you find it more expedient and efficient to show these reports to the public too so that people know what we are addressing here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would be glad if the usher could take out the first report and -- I'm sorry -- the report that is -- yes, the first report, the report that is found in tab 1. If you could put that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, Mr. Harmon, we have open sessions and we have to take care of that. Of course, the Judges need to see the reports, but perhaps the public should also see them. Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the report that's been found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 77 tab 1 has been placed on the ELMO. Can you identify that report as being either an UNMO report or an UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an UNMO report, as can be seen from the way it is written. It's from UNMO headquarters sector Bosnia-Herzegovina north-east 2, UNMO headquarters, BiH command. So it is an UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a date on that report, and can you point with the pointer where the date of this report is located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the date, which is the 6th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on a particular day did you send more than one report up your chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true, because we had to send the situation reports, and if something occurred in the course of time, we would send updates of the same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if the usher could take that particular item off of the ELMO and if we could place the Prosecutor's 77, tab 2, on the ELMO, we'll be able to make a distinction between the reports that are contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, sorry once again for interrupting you. I should like to ask the technicians to do the following: When the document is placed on the ELMO, if they could first show us the document in its entirety, and only after that to focus on the pertinent paragraph. Could you please show us the whole document? Thank you. This would be enough. Thank you very much. Sorry, Mr. Harmon, for this interruption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for purposes of future reference for both for counsel and for the Trial Chamber, so they can make a distinction, is the report that is now on the ELMO an UNMO report or an UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an UNPROFOR report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are the observations contained in that report based on observations of UNPROFOR personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true. It's based on UNPROFOR personnel and not necessarily anything to do with UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me just, for purposes of future reference and convenience, let me turn to the item that is found in Prosecutor's 77, tab 6. If that could be placed on the ELMO. This will be of assistance both to the Trial Chamber and to counsel when they review these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, this is an UNMO report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could zoom down on the UNMO report, please, to the top of the page. Right there is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see, Colonel, the top of the page, underneath the word "from," there is the letters DTG, and then there are a series of numbers with July 1995. Could you explain to the Judges what those numbers are and how to read those numbers in respect of this document and in other documents where similar numbers appear?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, DTG means date, time, group. It is different from the normal dates. In the military, the way we write, you start the date -- the DTG with the date. That is the date. Like, here you can see it was on the 8th [indicates]. Then the time. That is using a 24-hour clock. That is, now it was at 1430. And then the letter Bravo, that is, B, means the time zone. For example, like where we were, we were using a time zone Bravo, and I think it is the same even here. In Kenya, West Africa, we use Charlie. So there is a difference in the time zones. Then the JUL, that means it's July. That is the month. And then the 95 indicates the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you very much. I hope that will assist the Chamber when they have an opportunity to review the reports, and assist counsel as well, in what time these particular observations that are reflected in the reports are being made. Now, I don't intend to go through all of these reports with you, Colonel Kingori, because that would take more time than I think would be necessary, but let me ask you: Do the reports that are found in Prosecutor's 77, and which you've had an opportunity to review, do they accurately reflect the events, as you perceive them, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to -- first of all, can you tell us when the attack on the Srebrenica enclave started.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the attack on the enclave started on the 6th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you summarise the attack, the methods that were used and the targets of the attack?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that day, in the morning, what woke us up was the shelling. "Shelling," we are talking about the usage of heavy weapons, like artillery pieces, mortars, and all that. So that is what woke us up that morning. The attack was concentrated on that day on the village of Srebrenica and Potocari, and as far as I knew, there were no military targets in that area. Like, where they were hitting in Srebrenica, they were hitting on the roads, next to the hospital, near -- hitting houses and all that. As far as I know, there were no military targets in that area that they were targeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the intensity of the shelling over the three days that you were in Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can say is that it was very high. At times we could count over a hundred shells landing in the same place, be it at Srebrenica. You know, a continuous shelling of up to a hundred shells in the same area, and that is quite high intensity, considering the size of those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the hospital. What happened to the hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the hospital was missed, I think three times. Three shells missed the hospital just by a whisker sort of. We could sense that it could have been targeted in that due to the inaccuracy of the weapons, we thought that was the reason why they could not get a direct hit on the hospital, because the miss was just by a few metres, just by a few metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any damage inflicted on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, other than maybe broken -- okay, broken windows due to fragmentation, there was no serious damage on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the PTT building where you and Major Tetteh were headquartered, was that struck by artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the PTT building was not hit at that particular time, it was hit later, but it was missed several times. Some of the shells could land on the opposite side where there was a hill, and we could sense maybe they were also targeting that area, but we were missed that time, until much later after we had withdrawn to DutchBat Compound. That is when it was hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your assessment, Colonel Kingori, about this particular artillery attack over the days that you remained in Srebrenica? Against what kind of targets were these shells directed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the target, as far as we knew, as far as we could get when we were going out for our patrols during that period, was mainly the populous; that is, the personnel -- the people in that area, that is, the civilians. Because after shelling for some period, you know, targeting the houses in that particular village, they would wait for some time then shell the same place again. According to our own assessment, that meant that they were waiting for the people to come out to pick the injured and maybe check the damage and all that, and then they would hit them again when they're still there. So they wanted, as far as we were concerned, to get maximum casualties on the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think they were targeting civilians, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my opinion, the main reason was to make sure that they harassed these people in such a way that they are forced to leave the enclave, because as they had said earlier, they did not want the Muslims inside that enclave. They just wanted it for themselves; that is, the Serbs. So they just wanted to cause fear, panic, and force the Muslims to flee that enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you eventually leave Srebrenica town and go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did, and this was -- we actually tried to stay in that place. We wanted to be as close as possible to the concentration of the shelling so that we could report as objectively as possible, but a time came when we were also, you know, threatened. When we sighted a tank positioned in a direct line of fire, about two kilometres or so from our location, we felt we were directly threatened and they could get a direct hit on us, and we feared for our own safety and decided to leave, though even -- okay. I will not go to that part, but by the time we were leaving, the Muslims did not want us to leave, because they felt if we leave them, the Serbs would just come and overrun that place. They also thought that the Serbs were maybe not hitting that place as seriously as they would have done because of our presence; that is, the presence of the UNMOs in that particular place, and that if we left, now they will do whatever they wanted with that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure when Your Honour wants to take a break in time. I'm prepared to proceed. I just am unclear on the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just thinking of how to split the last part of the day. Maybe it's a good idea to have a break now. We still have a couple of issues pending which need discussion, so I think that it would be perhaps a good idea to finish the testimony of Colonel Kingori at 2.15, and then we will have 15 minutes left for our discussion. So we are going to have a 20-minute break now, after which we will continue with the testimony of Colonel Kingori. Let me just tell you that we cannot hear this witness later than 2.15, because we have to have 15 minutes for our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, let us continue until quarter past two, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, on the 9th of July you went to Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At approximately what time did you arrive in Potocari and where did you go in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: We left the PTT building around 1800 hours, and I think we arrived maybe 10, 15 minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Potocari, we went to the DutchBat Compound. That is where the Dutch Battalion was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the following day, the 10th of July, did you attempt to contact representatives from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we attempted. We tried that time, but we were unable to contact them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you contact and who were you trying to contact?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were trying to contact Major Nikolic through your interpreter Petar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to the 11th of July, the next day, and can you tell me and tell the Chamber approximately what time refugees started to arrive in and around Potocari on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the refugees started streaming in in the afternoon on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 11th of July, are you able to estimate how many refugees were in and around the UN Compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can remember is that inside the compound there were about 5.000 or so refugees, and outside there were actually more than that. It could have been even up to 7.000, 8.000, or even up to 10.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges your assessment of the composition of those refugees, the percentage of men to women, the ages of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the percentages -- I might not be very correct, but the men were fewer than the women. Let's say -- we can say it's about 80 per cent women and the other percentage men, and also that the men who were there were -- okay. Most of them are older people, you know, beyond fighting age, as I can say, and the others were just boys, young boys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there sufficient food, sufficient water for those refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we had problems with water and food. Water -- actually, at that time we did not have any to feed those people with, and they were very thirsty. Even when I said -- okay. In the DutchBat Compound we had some water, but those who were outside did not have any at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recall the weather conditions to be like on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 11th it was hot, very hot during the day, and in the evening it was very, very cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 11th of July, did you receive a telephone call from a representative from the Bosnian Serb side, either a telephone call or radio contact, some form of communication?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 11th, Petar tried to communicate to us, requesting for a meeting with Major Nikolic. That is now us and UNPROFOR. But when we requested the UN headquarters for approval, we were not allowed to go there for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The assessment of the situation at that time was that since the airstrikes had already been called for, maybe that could have been the reason why the BSA wanted to call us for a meeting, and maybe even hold us as human shields against the airstrikes so that they do not occur. And we feared also, and our UN headquarters, that is, the sector headquarters, also feared for that fact, because something like that had happened earlier in other sectors, and it is a risky business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see any Muslim fighters, Muslim people who were armed in and around the UN Compound in Potocari on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were several, many BSA soldiers who came there that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I said Serb soldiers, I made a mistake. I meant to say Muslim fighters. Did you see any Muslim fighters on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were no Muslims soldiers there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, was there any shelling in and around the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can remember, shelling was ongoing, even at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what areas were being shelled, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Potocari was a target and Srebrenica was also a target. And we could hear some rockets overflying us, going towards other parts of the enclave. But at least Potocari and Srebrenica were still being targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see where those rockets or where that artillery fire was hitting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of them we could see, because -- like, the ones which were falling around Potocari we could see. But the ones going beyond, we could not know where they were hitting. But at least for Srebrenica we had one interpreter who had gone there and who from there could tell us what was going on. At least Srebrenica was being hit also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to the next day, the 12th of July. Did you see the arrival of Bosnian Serb soldiers on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- well, let me ask you this question: Approximately what time do you recall they arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was in the morning section. If I can remember very well, it was in the morning section, and -- yes, they arrived in the morning section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldiers that you saw arriving into the Potocari area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the soldiers I remember seeing coming over there wore black -- they had black uniforms. They looked different from the normal BSA soldiers we used to see around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to those soldiers, did you see any other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also saw the normal, ordinary soldiers in green camouflage, and -- that is, their normal BSA camouflage -- and also there were some in blue, which was normally being used by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Muslim people when the Bosnian Serb soldiers arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the actual reaction was they were all afraid when they saw the soldiers passing through there. You could see fear in them, uncertainty. They did not know what will happen to them, because they were now in one place. And they were always -- they were afraid of the worst, you know, what could happen to them at that particular time. You could see it in their eyes, their reaction, the way they talked. They were all afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sometime on the 12th of July, did Bosnian Serb military representatives come to the UN Compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the circumstances under which they came and who came?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The ones who came in, they were just coming to check whether there were any Muslim soldiers inside there, Muslim soldiers, you know, whether they were armed or not. At least they were looking for Muslim soldiers inside there. Secondly, they wanted to see who is actually housed there, because when we met them, we told them it is only the injured people, the women and older men of Srebrenica who are inside there. And they sort of maybe did not trust what we told them, and they decided to go in and check for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there when these representatives from the Bosnian Serb army came?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was personally there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify any of the individuals who came to the UN Compound at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can. I can remember some of them. At least I can remember some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least there was Major Nikolic, he was there; the interpreter, Petar, was also there; Colonel Vukovic was also there; and there was -- Krstic was also there; another guy I cannot remember, another senior officer. I cannot remember his name very well. But I can remember some of their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've previously identified Petar. You said Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was introduced to us together with the other senior officers, and he was introduced as being one of the senior officers from the BSA side. And I cannot remember his actual position in that hierarchy. I can't remember that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen a picture of an individual who you have identified as Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that individual in this courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Mind if I stand up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: It's that individual there [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify what he's wearing, for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That time he was in green camouflage, but his weight was a bit -- difficult for me to identify him now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify what he's wearing now?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Right now he's in a black suit and a blue shirt and a dotted tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the record reflect, Mr. President, that the defendant has been identified by Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can have a seat, Colonel Kingori. Now, let me ask that -- let me ask you this question: Who introduced you to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, anyway, I didn't know him as a General at that time, but he was introduced to me by Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the individuals Major Nikolic, General Krstic, Petar, and others, remain with you in and around the UN Compound on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were together in that area, inside the compound, for about 15 minutes or so, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask -- you said you could not -- you didn't know the names of some of the others, but you could recognise them. Did I have an opportunity to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit number 28, and did you identify an individual from within this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/3.2 put on the ELMO, please. That's not 3.2. This is 3.2. It's under tab 1. It's under tab 1. You can use mine. Use this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify one of the individuals who you saw with General Krstic and Petar and Major Nikolic at the UN Compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This individual was there that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On this particular exhibit, Mr. President, the witness has pointed to the individual in the left-hand side of the photograph. Now, Mr. Usher, if you can give that back to me, I will show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/1. Do you see that same individual in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see him. He's the one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating the individual on the far left-hand side of that particular image.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, after the individuals left, did you have an opportunity to see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the circumstances under which you met General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: At that time, I saw some -- okay, the normal movement of the BSA soldiers now on the road adjacent to the DutchBat Compound, and I went out to check what was going on, normal routine just to see what was happening outside there. That is when I saw a group of BSA soldiers surrounding a certain individual, and I became a bit curious. Upon arriving there, I saw General Mladic, who I could identify, because I had seen him earlier on television, photos, and all that. So at least I could identify him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing? I'm sorry. What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: At that particular moment, he was -- I can't remember whether that is the time he was distributing -- yeah. That is the time he was distributing soft drinks and candies and all that to the refugees who were outside the main compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to General Mladic distributing sweets and drinks to the refugees, did you see anybody else doing that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were other senior officers and soldiers who were doing the same, the distribution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you, if I could, Prosecutor's Exhibit 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Mr. President, is a very short piece of film footage that has been seen previously. In order to shorten it, I have made this film footage. It is only a matter of seconds. But if we could play Prosecutor's Exhibit 78, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, it should come up on your monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you see that scene or scenes similar to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was there that time when that distribution was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what else you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: At that time, when the distribution was going on, there was someone with a video camera. At least he was filming whenever the distribution was going on. As far as I thought at that time, it was maybe a PR or, let's say, a propaganda issue. That is what I thought, that maybe they want to show the world that they are doing something for these people, and maybe the International Community could forget whatever they have done against those people. Also what I saw that time was immediately the camera turned to a different direction, some of the soldiers could pick the candies back, you know, from the people they have just given, the children and all that. So that is something unique. I did not understand why they had to do that. And that is -- that forced me to conclude that this is just a PR or personal relationship thing, maybe just to show the International Community that they are not against these Muslims per se.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not understand this last thing. You said -- what did you conclude when they picked back the sweets? What did you conclude? That it was not against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I concluded was that if they're picking these candies back from the individuals, the main purpose of giving them was to show, because the filming was going on, to show the International Community that they are doing good things to these refugees, so that the opinion of the International Community can forget or can ignore the atrocities they have already committed to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, did you see General Mladic on one occasion or more than one occasion on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: On the 12th, I saw him twice. I think twice, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The second occasion was when I realised that there was separation, separation going on between the men and the women and children. And men were being taken to a certain location, actually a house on the left side as you go from Srebrenica, actually out of Potocari. I did not understand why the separation was there. And also the way the men were being kept in that building was not in a good manner. There were very many. It was crowded. They were stepping on each other. The whole scenario did not look good to me, and that is why I went to General Mladic and asked him what is actually going on. Why are they doing something like that; that is, putting people together, huddling them together in such a small place, and all the men, why they were doing that. He told me, they don't have anything -- there's nothing bad they're doing. In fact, the people there are very comfortable. They're very comfortable inside there. Then he requested me to accompany him, but then there was a delay, a small delay. We went there with him, but that time some BSA soldiers had already gone towards the house, and when we arrived there, they started distributing beer, soft drinks to the men now. And he asked me, "Can't you see that they're comfortable? Can't you see?" just because they were taking the drink. "Can't you see that they're okay?" There's nothing that I had done, because I had earlier tried to go there and I was prevented. Now this time I requested him to allow me to enter the house, and he personally told me no, there is no point in going inside there. So there is practically nothing I could have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you said you tried to go into the house earlier. Who prevented you from going into the house where these men were being kept?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: BSA soldiers who were guarding that place. The place was being guarded by BSA soldiers. They were the ones who told me I cannot be allowed to go inside that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And as a result of that, you went to see General Mladic, I take it, and that's when he returned with you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Right. That is what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you also have another occasion to see General Krstic and other high-ranking officers that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to the Judges the circumstances under which you saw General Krstic and other high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was partly -- at the same time when we were with General Mladic, these guys were there. All of them, they were there and around. After that -- I cannot remember the other place where I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "these guys," who are the individuals you said are "these guys"? Can you identify them more precisely?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the people I'm talking about are the senior BSA soldiers -- BSA officers. We're talking about Major Nikolic, Colonel Vukovic -- the ones I can remember the names -- and also Krstic, and another person who introduced himself to me as the legal officer, a legal officer. Can I remember the name? Oskuminic or someone like that. But he told me he's a legal officer and even wrote his address for me, which I still keep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What language did the legal officer speak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the legal officer was speaking English, you know, fluent. Good English. Good English. That is why we were able to discuss with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph of Prosecutor's 28/13.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is found, Mr. Usher, in tab 11. That's it. Yes. Could you place that on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify this individual?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the guy who presented himself as the legal officer. I can remember him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the individual who was speaking English?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: And the person who was speaking English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, previously in this testimony you also identify an individual who was found at Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Usher, is found in tab 6. Place that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individual on the left-hand side of this Prosecutor's Exhibit, did you see him again that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was there. We were with him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also identified an individual who is in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which is found in tab 2, Mr. Usher. Place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individual you've previously identified in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4, did you see him as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He is the individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you in a position to see what the accused, General Krstic, and these individuals were doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: What I can remember very well was that they were coming in and going out. They were at one time with us and with General Mladic there, and at times they would go out there, I mean, to the soldiers, talk to them, which, as far as I was concerned, they were giving orders to these soldiers. Then they would later come back and join us or go to another place. So they were in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see the accused and these other individuals near the area where these Muslim men who had been separated were being detained?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we went there with General Mladic, these people were there. These -- we were together, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you if you can identify this particular location. Do you recognise that particular building?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that building?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This is the building we were calling White House. This is the place where the men were being taken to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there more than one building where the men were being taken to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was one of them. The other one was somewhere in a different location, but this was the place I said after the separation of the men were being handled together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 53/B [sic], which is a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask that that be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ask you, Colonel Kingori, if you can locate on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3B the second location where men were being detained.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not very easy to detect from here, but the other location was somewhere here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a pen, please -- there should be a pen available to you -- and would you circle the area where the second location is where the men were being detained?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Colonel. Now, did you actually see the men being separated, and did you see what happened to them when they approached one or both of these locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: If I can start with the White Building, I was personally there, and I saw the men being taken towards that building. They were being forced to leave their belongings at the road junction with the truck that leads to the building just somewhere there, all their belongings. By that I mean even the money they had, the pocketknives they had, their wallets, and any other belongings, maybe bags and all that. They were leaving all of them out there before they entered the building. As for the other house, the one I have just marked, the men who were being taken there, I was told by some Dutch soldiers that there were some men who had been taken behind that building, and they didn't know what was happening. So I decided to go inside there and check. The soldier, the Dutch soldiers do not go inside there but as an UNMO I could go in there. It's taking a risk obviously, but I went inside there, tried to go behind to see what was going on, but I was prevented from continuing by the Serb soldiers who were there. They told me -- they just showed me to go back, and I just retreated, and that was it at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I'm sorry for the interruption, but I saw in the transcript on page 92, 22nd line, it mentions the exhibit, your exhibit 53/B, and it should be corrected 5/3B. I believe one needs to pay attention because this marking, this kind of numbering could cause problems later on. It is not 53, it is 5/3, and I should like to ask either the court reporters or the interpreters or you to pay attention when exhibits are called out. I'm sorry for having to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you turn your attention, please, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/B -- I'm sorry, 5/3B. That is on the ELMO in front of you. You said you attempted to go into that particular area. And why was that again?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The reason why I wanted to go to that particular area was that the Dutch -- some Dutch soldiers had reported that men were being taken behind there, and were not returning. Whenever they were taken behind there, none of them was coming back. So mine was purely to go and investigate what was going on. And according to him, he told me that shooting was going on behind. There was some shooting. They could hear some shooting there. And so I went there to investigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear some shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I personally did. I heard some shooting when I tried -- when I attempted to go behind there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take your pointer, please, and indicate the area where you attempted to pass.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The place I attempted to pass was through here, behind these buildings [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating the buildings that are circled?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes. And that is where I could not be led through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the shooting point, where you heard the sounds of the shots coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not easy to detect, but it was at a close place; it was not far. Because the noise that was coming could -- you know, indicated that the shooting is not happening far from where I was. And it was -- if I can clarify, it was single shots; not bursts, but single shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Colonel Kingori: I'd like to return to some of your earlier testimony where you said that you personally saw Muslim males having their belongings taken out of their -- off their persons. Did that include their identifications?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I think one thing to say there is that it's not -- things were not being removed from their pocket. They were forced to remove them. And secondly, that that included the identification and everything. When an individual removed his items, whatever he had, then he would go ahead to another soldier who would physically search whether there is anything inside. But still, if there was anything, they were being forced -- they were being told to remove them and put them down. So this actually included even their identification cards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question, Colonel. Had you had a conversation with any representative of the Bosnian Serb army about what was going to happen to these particular men who had been separated?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked that, and the individual who answered me that question -- that is, the first question I had asked was: Why the separation? Then the second question was: What do they intend to do with these men after they separate them? And the answer was given by the person identified as -- having told me he was the legal officer, he told me that the reason why they are separating the men was for them to use them in exchange to their own prisoners of war who had been taken by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in light of what you saw, that is, identification papers and other personal effects being dropped on the ground, what conclusions, if any, did you come to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: It was a bit difficult now to know what was actually going on, but if you do not -- normally, if you don't want to have someone -- if you do not want someone to have an identification card, it literally means that maybe you don't want him in that way to identify himself or be identified by someone else, because that is the only thing -- that is, the ID card -- the only thing one can use to identify himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever go back and inform the person who was identified as the legal officer about why they were required to leave their identifications on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not ask him exactly, you know, that way, whether -- I mean, as you have put it, I did not put the question as such. The question I had asked was why they were being separated, but not why they were leaving their ID cards there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- how long did these separations last on the day of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it took quite some time. It took quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any buses that left the area with just men in them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That is correct. I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these men being taken from before they were put on the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two sets here. The main one was the men who were being taken from that white building, the ones who had been put together earlier. They were put on their own buses, different from the ones carrying the women and children, and we did not know where their destination was, though they were telling us they are going to take them, I think, to Zvornik or somewhere. But we did not -- they did not clarify in particular what they are going to do with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with any of the men, the Muslim men who had been put on those buses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was an emotional period. This was an emotional time, as far as I was concerned, because some of the men are people we had lived together with in that village, and they were being put in these buses. Even, you know, when they were lined up beside the road, they could cry and shout to us, requesting for assistance, asking us what we can do to help them. They could shout and say, "You know these people are going to kill us, and then you are not doing anything about it." And I mean, to us it was a bit emotional. It was very emotional. And also to them. You could see the fear. There was a lot of fear. They didn't know what would happen. They felt, you know, that they are definitely -- something bad was actually going to be done to them. You know, we could see it, and they could also shout about it. In fact, some of them I even tried to tell them with the literal language of theirs that I could use, telling them not to worry; we have been told where they were being taken to, that is -- what do you call this place? -- Zvornik, and then later on to Tuzla, and they should not fear. Because at least we had been assured nothing bad would happen to them. But you could see there was a lot of fear. They were crying. You know, men -- you can imagine men crying in front of you and seeking assistance from you, assistance which you cannot give. We, as individuals -- in fact, at that time I was, I think, the only UNMO there, and as an individual, there is no assistance I could have given. It was beyond -- it had gone beyond my control. And you could see them, you know, crying. It was quite emotional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, what was the age range of the males who had been separated and who had been placed in the White House and the other house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The men in the White House, those were the younger men, if I can say, because the others who were in the main DutchBat Compound were the older people, the very old, who some of them could hardly walk well. But these ones -- those ones in the White House were the younger, you know, slightly younger people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the youngest person you saw separated on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That time they were separating even some very young boys, some as young as 13, 14, and they were telling them to go and join the other men. And several instances I intervened and starting asking the boys, "What is your age?" They would tell me, "I'm 14." And then I would tell the soldiers, "These guys -- this boy is 14 years old. Why are you separating them?" And maybe that way they could allow them to continue. I saw another one, I could do the same. But immediately I turned from that direction and started -- they were still having the same boys, you know, to go and join the men. So I could not be able to cope with the situation. I could not prevent all the younger boys from me being separated, so some of them were actually taken together with the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you to turn your attention to the 13th of July. Did the separations that you've described witnessing on the 12th of July continue on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the separation process that you saw on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The separation on the 13th was just almost a continuation of what was happening earlier; it was only that now -- it was almost a continuation of the same, as I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, when you say "almost a continuation," were males separated and taken to one of the two locations that you've previously described, and were they forced to abandon their belongings at those locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: At this time no men were being taken to that -- to the White House, but at least they were still abandoning their belongings, they were being forced to leave their belongings. Because some of these at that time were those who were in the DutchBat Compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask that Prosecutor's Exhibit 75 be played. It's a film clip that lasts approximately three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you have seen this film clip before. You are in this film clip. And I'd like you to take a look at this film clip and then you can discuss with the Court your observations about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we could please play Prosecutor's Exhibit 75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the abandoned belongings, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the belongings which were abandoned by the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man in the blue vest, is that a Serb or a Dutchman?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That is a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these abandoned belongings as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, these are some of the belongings which were abandoned there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question about the man who you just identified as a Serb soldier. He was wearing a blue vest. Was that -- what kind of vest was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was a vest that we used to wear when we were there. It was bullet-proof. I don't you know what we can -- you know, some of them were not actually bullet-proof, but they were to protect our bodies, that is, the chest, from many small arms. And I'm sure it had been stolen from some of the Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges that particular part of the film clip that they have just seen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That particular part was when I noticed the separation, that is, when the men who were being removed from the group and being taken to the White House, and I decided to ask for permission -- I mean, decided to be taken there. I decided to request to be taken to that White House to see what is going on. So in fact I was talking to the Serb soldiers who were there, to take me up there to see what exactly was going on, to prove to them that something was really wrong inside there. Anyway, I was not allowed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know you had indicated 2.15 would be an appropriate time to break, and I therefore would suggest we conclude at this point so we can hear the motions and deal with the motions that have been raised by counsel. Colonel, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, you have not finished the examination-in-chief of this witness, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have about 10 more minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Colonel Kingori, we have to finish with your testimony for today. You will have to come back on Monday at 9.30. I hope you will have a possibility to enjoy a nice weekend in The Hague. Have a nice weekend, and we'll see you again on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I think it was your turn, actually. We have heard the Defence, we have heard their applications, and we were about to hear your response to the said applications. So I will give you the floor so that we can hear your position on the two applications that have been made by the Defence. Maybe you have also some other information that you can provide to us. Maybe some discussion has taken place in the meantime. Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There has been some discussion that has taken place. In respect of the first application made by the Defence, I understand that application to be that, one, as a matter of principle, the Defence is interested in obtaining additional time in order to permit them to investigate in the event that there is new material testified to by a witness that is not contained in a statement that has been provided to the Defence pursuant to the normal discovery rules. And the second part of their request is to permit the Defence to call back certain witnesses under those circumstances so that the Defence can question those witnesses about the new information after a proper investigation has been completed by the Defence. In respect of that motion, we have no objection to it in principle. We believe, however, Mr. President, that there should be an application made by the Defence on a case-by-case basis when the Defence deems that those certain circumstances have arisen. It's also our position that the showing that would be required by the Defence in order to either gain additional time for an investigation, or calling the witness back, would be, one, a demonstration that the material that needs to be investigated and was not provided previously is material to the Defence, and that after a showing of materiality, then the parties would have an opportunity to make their comments to the Court and the Court could then decide. But one additional condition, in our view, would be if the Defence already has this material and has been provided the material, and is not about information that's new and not contained in the statement, then there would be no opportunity to call back the witness. Cross-examination is the proper time to inquire about information that's contained in the statements. So to reiterate, if it's new information and it's material, we would urge the Court to consider it on a case-by-case basis and permit both sides to address the Court before rendering a decision. So in principle, on those conditions, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do you wish to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to make one thing clear. I think there is one slight difference between our two positions. We requested the same treatment, both in respect of the events that were not stated in witness statements, as well as for the witness statements that we received prior to the trial, and after the trial began. We requested the same treatment for both statements. This goes to the quality of the evidence that has been disclosed. As regards this other condition, the condition of a showing, of the necessity to make a good showing, showing of materiality, I think that this is contained in our material. I believe that we are quite clear in respect of that. Let me just try to broaden the point a little bit. We are requesting the same treatment in respect of events that were not contained in witness statements, as well as the events that are contained in witness statements, but the statements that have been received shortly prior to the beginning of the trial, or after the trial began. And we have to bear in mind, of course, both versions in English and in Serbo-Croatian language as provided by Rule 66. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. We will examine your application together with the response made here during the discussion, and I believe that the Chamber will soon be able to make its ruling, perhaps on Monday, but probably not at the beginning of the session. I'm telling you this because I myself cannot be present on Tuesday. So Judge Riad and Judge Wald will be sitting on Tuesday, and the session will be presided by Judge Riad. In view of that, I think that we have to try and make a ruling on Monday. And I don't forget that we have another ruling pending, which hasn't been made yet, because it has to be made by the full Chamber, which was not the case this week because the absence of Judge Patricia Wald. We have to wait for her and we will make both rulings next week. I hope that for the time being this is all, but I should perhaps tell you, I do not have my schedule here, but as regards the programme of the Chamber, we're trying really hard to establish, to the extent it is possible, a calendar until the end of the year, including, of course, the months of July, August, September, and up until the end of the year. We will probably have a recess. I think it will be -- anyway, I will provide you with specific information when I have it. However, as regards the following months, we will continue hearing this case until the week which begins on the 1st of May. We have already talked about it. After that, after that week, we will give you enough time to revise your work, to prepare your work, because we will be sitting in another case for at least three weeks in a row. I'm telling you this so that both parties can organise themselves, but I hope that on Monday I will be in a position to give you more precise information, even in respect of the latter half of the year. However, one must bear in mind that this is a provisional schedule. The organisation in itself is not an objective of work, it is simply a means of our work. It can be changed, it may be changed if it is necessary to do so. There are a number of things that cannot be foreseen, and we have to leave enough space, enough time to organise matters accordingly. I see that Mr. Harmon would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I didn't address yet, Mr. President, the second part of the motion that was made by the Defence, which was an application for more time because of what was, in fact, an omission in the B/C/S version of the amended indictment, and I think the record should contain or refer to the certificate and the nature of the error that was presented and which limited the Defence, my colleagues from the Defence, in understanding the full extent of the indictment, because as I understand it, and I have a copy of the certificate from the registrar, on the French and the English version, in paragraph 24, the word at the end of the sentence of paragraph 24, the word "included" was present, but in the B/C/S version of the amended indictment that was made available to my colleagues, the word "included" was omitted, and it is based on that omission that the Defence is requesting, as I understand their request, additional time to investigate three locations that have been testified about by Mr. Ruez, the first being Nova Kasaba; the second, Konjevic Polje; and the third, the Jadar River, the Defence believing that the list on the indictment that they received was an exclusive list, and in the French and English languages, the authoritative languages of that Tribunal, it was broader than that. Now, I'd like to make clear for the record, as we already argued this motion or a related motion to this, and I won't belabour the point, but the facts that underlined each of these three locations had been provided to the Defence. There were aerial images that were made under Rule 70(B) to the Defence. What the Defence did not see in our presentation, in Mr. Ruez's presentation, are a total of 12 photographs that are found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 13/1, 13/2, 14/5 through 8, 14/11, 17/2, 17/3, and 18/1. Those photographs obviously the Defence could have seen had they made an application for reciprocal discovery under Rule 66(B), but all the information they were entitled to see prior to the commencement of this trial on these particular areas they did see, and they did see that in a timely fashion. Having said that, Mr. President, if the Court deems it appropriate that because of the translation error additional time is required for my colleagues to investigate those areas, we certainly would not oppose any decision by this Chamber to allot them additional time, but I think the record has to be clear about the facts that we have made available to them prior to this unfortunate omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. You may be seated. Let me just remind you that the Chamber has already made a ruling in this matter. It was one of our rulings. I do not want to insist, but I just want to remind you that we do not work on an authoritative basis, and as soon as parties have their reasons for a particular motion, we can always try and revise our schedules. We're not slaves of an organisation or a calendar. I understand that the Defence needs some additional time to prepare itself. As soon as reasons can be explained and justified, the Chamber can exercise its authority in an appropriate matter. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon, for reminding us of this problem, but as regards the specific issues of the inclusion of the three locations, Nova Kasaba, Zeleni Jadar, and Konjevic Polje, the Chamber has already made a ruling. We will, of course, take into account what has been said here. We, in general, are mindful of the needs of the parties in respect of their respective preparations, and we will make another ruling in respect of that next week. All I can do at the end of this day is to wish you a nice weekend. Have a nice weekend, therefore, and we'll see you again on Monday, 9.30.
